design_detail: Retrospective case series from the London centre of the United Kingdom's National Poisons Information Service (NPIS). All documented telephone enquiries from December 1993 to November 1995 were screened by an information officer for MDMA use complicated by a serum sodium below 130 mmol/l, and clinical details and blood and urine results were requested from the hospital concerned. From December 1995 to March 1996, service medical staff gave management advice for acute cases and, where possible, asked for serial sodium and osmolality tests; blood and urine samples were obtained for toxicology at the authors' laboratory. One further fatal case, where the authors' advice was sought, is included; the paper says it has since been reported separately (reference 12). 17 patients are described: 15 who recovered (Table 1) and 2 who died (Table 2). Descriptive only: there is no comparison group and no statistical analysis is described (Methods, p. 434).
can_establish: What the picture looked like in 17 young people who developed low blood sodium after taking MDMA and whose cases reached a poisons service over about two years: what the hospital records said they had taken and drunk, how soon they became ill, their sodium and urine tests, the course over the next days and the two deaths; and that no raised temperature is recorded for any of the 17.
cannot_establish: How often low sodium follows MDMA (the 17 cases come from telephone enquiries, not from a count of people who took MDMA); who is at greater risk (no comparison group); whether the amount of fluid or the amount of MDMA brought it on (fluid histories are approximate or missing, and nobody who drank similarly and stayed well is described); or whether MDMA raised vasopressin in these patients (it was not measured in this series).

sample.recruitment: Telephone enquiries to one poisons service's London centre. Screened retrospectively from December 1993 to November 1995; from December 1995 to March 1996, cases arising from requests for management advice; plus one further fatal case where the authors' advice was sought, which the paper says has since been reported (Methods, p. 434; reference 12, whose first author is one of this paper's authors).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MDMA use associated with hyponatraemia, defined as serum sodium below 130 mmol/l; no other criteria are given (Methods, p. 434).
sample.demographics: Seven men and ten women aged 15 to 26. Among the 15 who recovered: 7 men and 8 women. Both who died were female, aged 15 and 18 (Table 1, pp. 432-433; Table 2, p. 435).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; an outcome is given for all 17. Many cells of Table 1 are empty and the paper does not say whether the test was not done or not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Only people whose doctors telephoned the poisons service are included; people with milder low sodium, or whose hospital did not call, are absent, and so is anyone who drank a lot and stayed well. The authors themselves say complications of MDMA may be under-reported (Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 434).

exposure.measurement: Tablets and fluids as recorded in the clinical details requested from the hospital concerned (Methods, p. 434); the paper does not say who supplied the history. MDMA was confirmed analytically in 8 of the 15 who recovered, and in blood in both who died (0.05 and 0.209 mg/l). A fluid history was not available for 5 of the 15 who recovered (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 434; Tables 1 and 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As recorded in the hospital reports, not a study condition. Among the 13 who recovered and had a stated amount, 12 had taken two tablets or fewer (one had taken three); both who died had taken one tablet, and both had taken MDMA before. Tablet content was not measured (a Table 2 footnote gives only a general range for tablets). Every patient became ill within 12 hours of taking the drug, and the two who died within about 5 hours (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 434; Results, p. 434; Table 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol was drunk by several patients (beer, wine, gin; blood ethanol 0.8 g/l in one of the two who died); one of those who died (the 18-year-old) had smoked cannabis. The authors say they do not know whether the patients smoked tobacco, which matters because nicotine releases vasopressin (Table 1; Table 2; Discussion, pp. 435-436).

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Everything that might explain who becomes ill: body weight, kidney function, previous MDMA use, exertion, room temperature, sweat loss, and how many people drank similar amounts and stayed well.

outcomes.instruments: Serum sodium and calculated serum osmolality, urine osmolality (and urine sodium in one patient) from hospital laboratories; presenting features, Glasgow Coma Scale, scans, treatment and outcome from hospital notes; post-mortem findings in the two who died; toxicology at the authors' laboratory (Methods and Results, p. 434; Tables 1 and 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Serum osmolality was calculated from sodium, potassium, urea and glucose in many patients (footnote c of Table 1). The SIADH pattern is defined as low sodium, low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 434).
outcomes.operationalization: A case is an enquiry in which MDMA use was complicated by serum sodium below 130 mmol/l; the series reports what the patients had taken and drunk, their presenting features, sodium and osmolality values and outcome.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None; data were abstracted from hospital reports after the event.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts only. Of 17: 7 men, 10 women; ages 15-26; serum sodium 107-128 mmol/l on day 1 (Table 1 and Table 2); 2 deaths. Of the 15 who recovered (counted on the rendered Table 1, pp. 432-433): MDMA confirmed in the laboratory in 8; 8 known to have drunk a large amount of fluid (water, soft drinks or beer) and 5 with no usable fluid history; seizures in 10; 13 labelled complete recovery, 1 with poor concentration and short-term memory at 2 months after a head injury (extradural haematoma and skull fracture), and 1 needing a tracheostomy after aspiration. Biochemistry fitted SIADH in 6 patients. The abstract gives 10 confirmed, 10 known large fluid intake, 11 with seizures and 14 complete recoveries; the first three equal the text counts plus the patients who died (see reporting issues). Share of ecstasy enquiries: 135 a month of 13,762 enquiries; 17 cases in 28 months, which the paper gives as 0.4% of enquiries about ecstasy (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 434).
analysis.selective_reporting: Descriptive series without hypotheses; cases are selected by their outcome (low sodium), so nothing can be said of those who drank and took MDMA without becoming ill.

interpretation_gap.results_show: 17 young people, 10 of them women, became ill with low blood sodium within 12 hours of taking MDMA (12 of the 13 survivors with a stated amount had taken two tablets or fewer; each of the two who died had taken one). 8 of the 15 survivors were known to have drunk a large amount of fluid and the history was not available for 5; both who died had drunk a large amount of water. Illness began with vomiting and disturbed behaviour, then drowsiness and agitation, with seizures in 10 of the 15 survivors and drowsiness, mutism or disorientation for up to 3 days. No raised temperature is recorded for any of the 17. 15 recovered (13 labelled complete recovery) and 2 died of brain swelling. In 6 patients the sodium, serum osmolality and urine osmolality fitted the pattern the authors call SIADH.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary and Discussion state that MDMA can cause life-threatening hyponatraemic encephalopathy when accompanied by excessive fluid ingestion, that the mechanism involves inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone, and, at the end, that the hyperthermic and hyponatraemic complications appear largely avoidable. The cases are consistent with a link to a large fluid intake, but a series with no comparison group cannot show cause or avoidability, and vasopressin was not measured in these patients; the Discussion itself says the way MDMA causes the hormone release remains to be established (p. 435).

timeline.event: Earliest report of low sodium with stupor after ecstasy in this paper's reference list (Maxwell, Polkey and Henry; reference 10).

A near-fatal case attributed to vasopressin over-secretion (Holden and Jackson; reference 7) and cerebral oedema after unrestricted water intake (Matthai and colleagues; reference 9), as cited by this paper.
A rise in vasopressin after MDMA in eight healthy men (Henry and colleagues; reference 19), as cited by this paper; not read here.
This series: 17 cases from one poisons service, 2 deaths.
A series of 18 people with low sodium after ecstasy, 17 of them women (Budisavljevic and colleagues), as cited in the California series; not read here.
California poison-centre review of 545 reports: 73 with a recorded low sodium, 4 deaths among them.
Narrative review that tabulates published cases of low sodium after ecstasy.

replication.where_it_stands: The same picture, low sodium within hours of taking MDMA, usually with a large fluid intake, was described in earlier case reports (this paper cites about eight) and later in a larger American poison-centre series and a review of published cases, both read in this batch. None of the studies read here compares people who drank a large amount with people who did not, so the size of the risk and the part played by fluid remain untested.

funding.declared_conflicts: Not stated: no funding or competing-interest statement is printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from hospitals in Dundee, London and Chelmsford, one address in Sydney, and Imperial College. The last author (Henry) also wrote or co-wrote three of the papers this one cites, including the 1998 report of vasopressin after MDMA (reference 19), and one author (Parr) is first author of reference 12, a report of one of the fatal cases in this series.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective registry of everyone attending events or emergency departments after taking MDMA, with sodium measured on arrival, an account of fluids drunk, and a denominator, so that low sodium could be compared across levels of fluid intake, body size and sex; and studies in healthy volunteers that follow sodium, vasopressin and recorded fluid intake over the hours after MDMA.

domains.note: No comparison group: nobody who took MDMA and drank similarly and stayed well, so fluid, MDMA and every other difference are untestable.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Cases found through telephone enquiries to one service, by different routes in two periods, with one further fatal case added because advice was sought.
MDMA confirmed in the laboratory in 8 of 15 survivors; fluid intake by history, approximate, and missing for 5.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Not a trial; treatments were those the hospitals chose and are not the subject of the series.
Many sodium, osmolality and urine values are blank in Table 1; the SIADH pattern could be judged in only 6 patients.
Sodium is a laboratory value; clinical descriptions come from notes requested from the hospitals, and for the two deaths the first sodium was recorded after treatment had started.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Descriptive series with no tests; the abstract counts (10, 10, 11, 14) do not match the tables (8, 8, 10, 13) except by adding the two deaths.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A descriptive series appraised with ROBINS-I as the library does for other case series; it has no comparison group, so the confounding domain is critical by design. It can be cited for what these 17 cases looked like and what they were recorded as having taken and drunk; it cannot be cited for how often it happens, for who is at risk, or for fluid or MDMA as the cause.

key_findings.finding: Case finding: of a mean 13,762 enquiries a month to the service, 135 a month (1.0%) concerned ecstasy; over the 28-month study period 17 cases of low sodium after MDMA were identified, which the paper gives as 0.4% of enquiries about ecstasy: 7 men and 10 women aged 15-26. The percentage is a share of telephone enquiries, not of people who took MDMA.

Presentation: vomiting and disturbed behaviour, then drowsiness and agitation, with seizures in 10 of the 15 who recovered; drowsiness, a mute state and disorientation for up to 3 days; the authors say clinical findings did not necessarily reflect the size of the sodium fall. Serum sodium on day 1 was 107-128 mmol/l. Temperature was recorded as normal in 12 of the 15 who recovered, as 37.5 degrees Celsius in two and 34.8 in one; at hospital presentation it was 32.6 and 33 degrees in the two who died.

Fluid and tablets: 8 of the 15 who recovered were known to have drunk a large amount of water, soft drinks or beer, and for 5 the fluid history was not available; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken two tablets or fewer. Both who died had taken one tablet and had drunk an excessive amount of fluid.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, 'History of MDMA and fluid ingestion' column (pp. 432-433); Results, 1st paragraph and top of right column (p. 434); Table 2 (p. 435)

key_findings.finding: The two deaths, both female and both having taken MDMA before: a 15-year-old (one tablet at midnight; dancing, talking and drinking water, at least 3 litres, in rotation; ill at 05:00 and given a considerable amount of water; serum sodium 125 mmol/l at 12:00 after 1.5 litres of intravenous fluid and 1 litre of saline; brain swelling and herniation; brain dead on day 2; blood MDMA 0.05 mg/l) and an 18-year-old (one tablet at 19:45; smoking cannabis and some alcohol; water from 22:00; ill at 00:15 and drank 6-7 cups of water; serum sodium 126 mmol/l; marked brain swelling; brain dead on day 3; blood MDMA 0.209 mg/l, MDA 0.029 mg/l, ethanol 0.8 g/l). Symptoms of brain swelling began within 5 hours of taking one tablet.

Outcome of the 15 who recovered: 13 are labelled complete recovery in Table 1; one had difficulty in concentration and poor short-term memory at 2 months after an extradural haematoma and skull fracture; one needed a tracheostomy after aspiration pneumonia and tracheitis.

Biochemistry consistent with SIADH (low sodium, low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine) in 6 patients. The authors say the low sodium appears to result from water consumption in excess of the body's requirements, compounded by failure of the kidney's response to a water load, and that the way MDMA causes SIADH remains to be established. A raised vasopressin in one earlier patient, and a rise in vasopressin after MDMA in eight healthy men, are cited from other papers.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 434); Discussion, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (p. 434) and p. 435, left column

key_findings.finding: The authors say that the early public message to those taking MDMA to 'drink plenty of fluids' was aimed at preventing overheating and did not state that a high fluid intake could be harmful without prolonged exertion, and that this was later corrected after publicity about the deaths. They also say symptoms of low sodium came on over a short space of time, and that recovery fitted clearing of MDMA and its metabolite over 24-48 hours.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'The acute onset of symptoms' and the paragraph on early public messages that follows it (p. 436, left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the text count differently. Confirmation of MDMA in 10 patients (abstract) against 8 (text and Table 1); a large fluid intake known in 10 against 8; seizures in 11 against 10. These equal the text counts plus the patients who died (2, 2 and 1), which the paper never says, and no denominator is given. The abstract's 14 complete recoveries do not match the 13 labelled complete recovery in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the text and table counts (8, 8, 10 and 13 of the 15 who recovered); the abstract mixes denominators of 15 and 17.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives a single window, December 1993 to March 1996, for screening all enquiries. The Methods describe screening of all documented enquiries only to November 1995, then, to March 1996, cases arising from requests for management advice with serial tests asked for, plus one further fatal case added because the authors' advice was sought.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cases were found by different routes, so the 17 cases and the two deaths cannot be read as a systematic count.

reporting_issues.issue: The share '0.4% of all enquiries about ecstasy' is the number of cases over the number of telephone enquiries.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is not a risk among people who take MDMA and should not be quoted as one.

reporting_issues.issue: For the 15-year-old who died, the sodium of 125 mmol/l was recorded at 12:00, after 1.5 litres of intravenous fluid on transport and 1 litre of 0.9% saline in hospital; for the 18-year-old the 126 mmol/l entry and the saline are in the same cell, so the order is not clear. The paper gives no pre-treatment values for either. Both are higher than several survivors (107 to 118), and the authors say clinical findings did not necessarily reflect the size of the fall.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sodium values recorded for the two deaths may be higher than before treatment and should not be used to compare severity with the survivors.

reporting_issues.issue: Fluid amounts are approximate. One entry carries a question mark (excessive amount of water, 13 bottles?); 'excessive amount' is not defined; several entries give an unknown amount.
reporting_issues.consequence: No dose-response between fluid and sodium can be built from this table.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence saying plasma vasopressin was found inappropriately raised 9 hours after ingestion in one case cites reference 1, which is titled as a report of a fatality with coagulopathy and hyperthermia; the near-fatal case with vasopressin over-secretion is listed as reference 7.
reporting_issues.consequence: The citation for the one earlier vasopressin measurement appears to be wrong; it cannot be traced from the paper alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The received and revised dates are printed in the wrong order (received 2 November 2002, revised 21 February 2002).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the findings; one date is a misprint.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 431-437 (PDFs/MDMA/Hartung_2002_HyponatraemicStates.pdf), full text: summary, Methods, Results, Tables 1 and 2, Discussion and references. Table 1 prints rotated; its rows were read and counted on rotated renders of printed pages 432 and 433 (8 laboratory confirmations, 10 seizures, 13 labelled complete recoveries among the 15), and the less-than sign in the case definition (lost in the text layer) was checked on the rendered pages.
